articles.title: The volunteers risking their lives to defuse Indonesia's wildfire 'carbon bombs'
articles.summary: Peat fires in Borneo are releasing ancient stores of carbon - and sending a toxic smog across South East Asia.
articles.content:
The sky grows heavy in Borneo, though not with rain. The air, amber-hued and treacle-thick, is smudged under a blanket of smog that has spilled across international borders – to Singapore, Manila, Kuala Lumpur.

Down on the ground, smoke steams from the soil.

It's like tear gas, says Dwi Sujatmoko.

"It hits your nose straight away, your eyes burn – that's more or less what it's like," he says. "People say these fires are extraordinary because of the flames and the smoke. And they're right."

The 35-year-old volunteer firefighter has spent more than a month enveloped in this haze, breathing toxic millennia-old microparticles of carbon as he toils against a seemingly inextinguishable fire front.

Using hand tools, carts and portable fire pumps, he and thousands of other volunteer firefighters – many of them indigenous Dayak or Banjar people – are up against an inferno that has carbonised some 200,000 hectares of forest and farmland across Indonesian Borneo since early July.

Underground and out of sight, giant subterranean peat fires continue to smoulder, choking the air with poisonous fumes.

"Once a fire becomes uncontrolled, it harms many people. Not just humans, but also animals and plants," Sujatmoko says. "If underground fire spreads and can no longer be controlled, the losses are enormous."
articles.reasoning: The article highlights the courageous efforts of volunteer firefighters combating massive peat fires in Indonesian Borneo, which have significant environmental and public health impacts. The story focuses on a meaningful and large-scale environmental crisis with broad regional effects, and the volunteers' actions represent a positive, impactful response to mitigate damage and protect ecosystems and communities.
articles.personality_title: Volunteers battle giant peat fires to protect Borneo’s forests and air
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Peat fires in Borneo, Indonesia, have burned large areas of forest and farmland since July. These fires release old carbon stored underground and create thick, harmful smoke that spreads across Southeast Asia, affecting air quality in cities like Singapore and Kuala Lumpur.

**What happened** – Thousands of volunteer firefighters, including local indigenous people like the Dayak and Banjar, have been working for over a month to control these fires. Using hand tools, carts, and portable pumps, they fight underground peat fires that are hard to see but produce dangerous smoke and damage the environment.

**Impact** – These peat fires are especially harmful because they release ancient carbon, worsen air pollution, and threaten plants, animals, and people. The volunteers’ work helps slow the spread of the fires, reducing the damage to the land and the health risks from the smoke.

**What’s next step** – Continued efforts by volunteers and local communities will be needed to fully control the fires. Their work could help prevent similar disasters in the future and protect the region’s forests and air quality.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Brave volunteers are fighting tough peat fires in Borneo to reduce environmental damage and protect people’s health across Southeast Asia.
articles.personality_title_fr: Des bénévoles combattent les feux de tourbe géants pour protéger les forêts et l’air de Bornéo
articles.personality_presentation_fr:

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Des milliers de pompiers volontaires, dont des populations indigènes locales comme les Dayak et Banjar, travaillent depuis plus d’un mois pour maîtriser ces feux. Avec des outils manuels, des chariots et des pompes portables, ils combattent des feux de tourbe souterrains difficiles à voir, mais qui produisent une fumée dangereuse et endommagent l’environnement.

**Impact** – Ces feux de tourbe sont particulièrement nuisibles car ils libèrent du carbone ancien, aggravent la pollution de l’air et menacent les plantes, les animaux et les humains. Le travail des bénévoles aide à ralentir la propagation des feux, réduisant ainsi les dégâts sur la terre et les risques sanitaires liés à la fumée.

**Prochaine étape** – Les efforts continus des bénévoles et des communautés locales seront nécessaires pour maîtriser complètement les feux. Leur travail pourrait aider à éviter de futurs désastres similaires et à protéger les forêts et la qualité de l’air dans la région.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Des bénévoles courageux combattent de puissants feux de tourbe à Bornéo pour limiter les dégâts environnementaux et protéger la santé des populations en Asie du Sud-Est.
articles.personality_title_es: Voluntarios luchan contra grandes incendios de turba para proteger los bosques y el aire de Borneo
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Los incendios de turba en Borneo, Indonesia, han quemado grandes áreas de bosque y tierras agrícolas desde julio. Estos incendios liberan carbono antiguo almacenado bajo tierra y producen un humo denso y dañino que se extiende por el sudeste asiático, afectando la calidad del aire en ciudades como Singapur y Kuala Lumpur.

**Qué pasó** – Miles de bomberos voluntarios, incluidos pueblos indígenas locales como los Dayak y Banjar, han estado trabajando durante más de un mes para controlar estos incendios. Usan herramientas manuales, carretillas y bombas portátiles para combatir incendios subterráneos de turba que son difíciles de ver pero que producen humo peligroso y dañan el medio ambiente.

**Impacto** – Estos incendios de turba son especialmente dañinos porque liberan carbono antiguo, empeoran la contaminación del aire y amenazan a plantas, animales y personas. El trabajo de los voluntarios ayuda a frenar la propagación de los incendios, reduciendo el daño a la tierra y los riesgos para la salud por el humo.

**Próximo paso** – Se necesitarán esfuerzos continuos de voluntarios y comunidades locales para controlar completamente los incendios. Su trabajo podría ayudar a prevenir desastres similares en el futuro y proteger los bosques y la calidad del aire en la región.

**Frase clave** – Voluntarios valientes luchan contra difíciles incendios de turba en Borneo para reducir daños ambientales y proteger la salud en el sudeste asiático.

articles.title: Turtle doves released in bid to stop extinction
articles.summary: Conservationists release more than two dozen turtle doves in the South Downs National Park.
articles.content:
Conservationists have released more than two dozen turtle doves in the South Downs National Park in a bid to help the species, which is on the brink of extinction in the UK, to recover.

The dove, famous for its place in the Twelve Days of Christmas song, is the country's fastest declining bird species according to the RSPB.

In an attempt to boost population numbers, the national park authority released 30 birds in the Selborne area of Hampshire this spring.

The authority said the plan was part of "urgent efforts" to restore the species, with a further 100 doves being prepared for another release next year.

"We all know the turtle dove from the festive carol, but the truth is they are now far too rare for such a Christmas gift," park ranger Paul Bushell said.

He explained the birds were now "one of the fastest-declining bird species in Europe", with numbers plummeting by 98% in the UK between the late 1960s and 2023.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a concrete conservation effort to prevent the extinction of the turtle dove, a species experiencing a dramatic population decline in the UK. The release of birds in a national park and plans for further releases represent meaningful, tangible action with broad environmental significance. The story is focused and provides sufficient context about the species' decline and recovery efforts.
articles.personality_title: Turtle doves released to help save UK population from extinction
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Turtle doves, known from the Christmas song “The Twelve Days of Christmas,” are facing a big problem in the UK. Their numbers have dropped by 98% since the late 1960s, making them one of the fastest-declining birds in Europe.

**What happened** – This spring, conservationists released 30 turtle doves in the South Downs National Park, located in Hampshire. This is part of urgent efforts to help the species recover. The park authority plans to release another 100 birds next year.

**Impact** – This effort is important because turtle doves are very rare now and could disappear completely from the UK if nothing is done. Releasing these birds into a protected area gives them a better chance to survive and breed.

**What's next step** – The next step is to release more birds in the coming year and continue monitoring their progress. The hope is that these actions will help the population grow again and prevent extinction.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Conservationists are actively releasing turtle doves in a UK national park to stop their rapid decline and help save the species from extinction.

articles.title: Hot summer helps group clear 'buckets' of lake litter
articles.summary: The hot summer has meant lakes and rivers across the country have been running low.
articles.content:
Volunteers in a north Shropshire town have been able to litter pick inside a prominent lake because its water levels have dropped due to the recent hot weather.

With this summer being the hottest and one of the driest on record, lakes and rivers across the country have been running low.

It has meant Ellesmere park ranger, Lee Fraser, has been able to go into the Mere with volunteers and pick out litter, such as bricks, pottery and mobile phones.

He said the team have already collected "five big bucket loads" of litter which he said "covered half the distance" of the town's promenade.

Fraser said this year they decided to collect litter by standing in the water, as it was easier to see what was in the water.

"We tried it last year from a boat, which when you stand on the bank, you can see all the bricks.

"Once in the water, on the boat, even if you are next to them and someone's shouting that it's right next to you, you cannot find it.

"There are quite a lot of bricks out on the side now already and we have only been at it less than an hour", he said.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a positive environmental action where volunteers are removing litter from a lake, improving local water quality and ecosystem health. The activity benefits the community and environment, with clear context and tangible impact. Although the hot summer causing low water levels is a concern, the focus is on the constructive cleanup effort.
articles.personality_title: Volunteers remove buckets of litter from lake during dry summer
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – This summer has been very hot and dry, causing lakes and rivers across the country to have much lower water levels than usual.

**What happened** – In Ellesmere, a town in north Shropshire, volunteers joined park ranger Lee Fraser to pick up litter from inside the town’s lake, called the Mere. Because the water was low, they could stand in the lake and find trash like bricks, pottery, and even mobile phones. They collected five large buckets of rubbish in less than an hour.

**Impact** – Cleaning litter from the lake helps keep the water and environment healthier for plants, animals, and people. Being able to stand in the water made it easier to see and remove trash than their previous method of using a boat. This effort improves the local area and shows how volunteers can make a big difference.

**What's next step** – The volunteers plan to continue their cleanup work as long as water levels allow. Their success might inspire other communities to organize similar lake and river cleanups, especially during dry periods when litter is easier to spot.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Thanks to low water levels from a hot summer, volunteers in Ellesmere have cleared large amounts of litter from the lake, improving the local environment.
articles.personality_title_fr: Des bénévoles retirent des seaux de déchets d’un lac pendant un été sec
articles.personality_presentation_fr:

**Ce qui s’est passé** – À Ellesmere, une ville dans le nord de Shropshire, des bénévoles ont aidé le garde du parc Lee Fraser à ramasser des déchets dans le lac de la ville, appelé le Mere. Grâce au faible niveau d’eau, ils ont pu se tenir dans le lac et trouver des déchets comme des briques, de la poterie, et même des téléphones portables. Ils ont collecté cinq grands seaux de déchets en moins d’une heure.

**Impact** – Nettoyer les déchets du lac aide à garder l’eau et l’environnement plus propres pour les plantes, les animaux et les habitants. Pouvoir se tenir dans l’eau a rendu plus facile la détection et le ramassage des déchets comparé à leur méthode précédente en bateau. Cet effort améliore la région locale et montre comment les bénévoles peuvent faire une grande différence.

**Prochaine étape** – Les bénévoles prévoient de continuer leur nettoyage tant que le niveau d’eau le permet. Leur succès pourrait encourager d’autres communautés à organiser des nettoyages similaires des lacs et rivières, surtout pendant les périodes sèches où les déchets sont plus visibles.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Grâce au faible niveau d’eau causé par un été chaud, des bénévoles à Ellesmere ont nettoyé une grande quantité de déchets dans le lac, améliorant l’environnement local.
articles.personality_title_es: Voluntarios recogen cubos de basura de un lago durante verano seco
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Este verano ha sido muy caluroso y seco, lo que ha provocado que los niveles de agua en lagos y ríos del país estén mucho más bajos de lo normal.

**Qué pasó** – En Ellesmere, un pueblo del norte de Shropshire, voluntarios se unieron al guardabosques Lee Fraser para recoger basura dentro del lago del pueblo, llamado Mere. Debido al bajo nivel de agua, pudieron pararse en el lago y encontrar basura como ladrillos, cerámica e incluso teléfonos móviles. Recogieron cinco cubos grandes de basura en menos de una hora.

**Impacto** – Limpiar la basura del lago ayuda a mantener el agua y el medio ambiente más saludables para las plantas, animales y personas. Poder estar dentro del agua facilitó ver y quitar la basura, comparado con su método anterior desde un bote. Este esfuerzo mejora la zona local y muestra cómo los voluntarios pueden hacer una gran diferencia.

**Próximo paso** – Los voluntarios planean continuar con la limpieza mientras el nivel de agua lo permita. Su éxito podría inspirar a otras comunidades a organizar limpiezas similares de lagos y ríos, especialmente durante períodos secos cuando la basura es más visible.

**Frase clave** – Gracias a los bajos niveles de agua por un verano caluroso, voluntarios en Ellesmere han recogido grandes cantidades de basura del lago, mejorando el ambiente local.
